client: I’ve been feeling really overwhelmed since starting college last semester. I can’t seem to keep up with my coursework no matter how hard I try, and it’s making me feel like I’m failing. I’ve started avoiding my friends because I’m embarrassed about falling behind, but now I just feel lonely on top of everything else. Honestly, I’m not sure if therapy can really help me with this—it feels like I’m just not cut out for college.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a heavy load of self-doubt along with your coursework, and that isolation must be making everything feel even harder. I hear how exhausted and discouraged you feel—would you be willing to explore together what thoughts come up when you tell yourself "I'm not cut out for college"?

client:
I don't know...when I think "I'm not cut out for college," it just feels like the truth. Everyone else seems to get the material so easily while I'm struggling just to keep up. I try to tell myself I can do it, but then I see my grades and it just confirms that I'm not smart enough. 

It's hard to explore those thoughts because they don't feel like thoughts—they feel like facts. Like I'm just facing reality about my limitations.
therapist: That sense of certainty in your thoughts must feel so heavy, like you're seeing concrete proof of your limitations everywhere you look. I wonder if we could gently examine what "smart enough" looks like to you—do you think there might be room for different kinds of intelligence beyond just keeping up with the pace?

client: I get what you're saying about different kinds of intelligence, but when I'm in meetings at work and can't think fast enough to contribute, it just feels like proof I'm not cut out for this. My mind goes blank and then I spend the whole night replaying every awkward silence, beating myself up about it. Even if other types of intelligence exist, they don't seem to matter in my actual daily struggles.
therapist: I hear how painful and real this experience feels for you in those moments when your mind goes blank. That immediate sense of falling short can be so convincing—what do you think might happen if we looked at those awkward silences with the same curiosity you'd extend to a friend who froze in a meeting?

client: I get what you're saying about treating myself like I would a friend, but it's not that simple. When I freeze up, all I can think is how everyone must be judging me, and that makes me freeze even more. Being curious about it just feels like another way to overanalyze my failures.
therapist: It sounds like that critical inner voice gets louder precisely when you most need compassion, making it incredibly hard to step back from those painful moments. What do you notice happens physically when you start worrying about others judging you—does your body react in any particular way?

client: I notice my chest gets really tight, like I can't take a full breath. And my hands start shaking a little, which makes me even more self-conscious because then I worry people will notice. It's frustrating because logically I know most people aren't actually judging me, but my body reacts like it's a real threat.
therapist: That mind-body connection is so powerful—your body responding as if there's real danger when your logical mind knows otherwise. Would it feel safe to explore how we might help your nervous system recognize that these work situations aren't actually threats?

client:
I get what you're saying about the mind-body connection, but when I'm in those stressful work meetings, it doesn't feel like something I can just logic my way out of. My heart races and my hands shake before I even realize what's happening. It's like my body takes over before my brain can catch up. 

I've tried telling myself "it's not a real threat" in the moment, but that just makes me feel worse because then I'm failing at calming myself down on top of everything else. It all feels so automatic and out of my control.
therapist: I hear how frustrating it feels when your body reacts before you can even think, and how added pressure to "fix" it in the moment just compounds the stress. What do you notice about the moments right before these physical reactions start—are there any tiny clues your body gives you that might help us catch this pattern earlier?

client: I never really thought about looking for early warning signs before. I guess sometimes my hands get a little shaky first, but by then it feels too late to stop it. It's frustrating because even if I notice something, the anxiety still takes over so fast.
therapist: It sounds like you're already starting to tune into those subtle physical cues, which is an important first step—even if it feels like things move quickly once they start. What do you think about experimenting with some grounding techniques during those early moments when you first notice your hands shaking?

client: I don't know... when my hands start shaking, everything feels so overwhelming already. Trying to do some technique in that moment seems impossible—like trying to read an instruction manual while your house is on fire. Part of me wants to try, but another part thinks it's just going to make me feel worse when I inevitably fail at it.
therapist: I hear how overwhelming that moment feels—like there's no space to even think about trying something new when everything feels like it's already falling apart. Would it feel safe to explore this together, starting with just noticing and naming what's happening, without any pressure to fix it in those moments?

client: I guess it could feel safe to just notice and name what's happening, but I’m not sure how much it would help. When everything feels like it’s falling apart, just naming it doesn’t make the chaos go away. It feels like I’m stuck in this cycle, and I don’t see how acknowledging it changes anything.
therapist: You're absolutely right that simply naming what's happening won't magically make the chaos disappear—that frustration makes complete sense when you're in the thick of these overwhelming moments. I wonder if we could explore together how noticing might create just enough space to breathe before we work on changing anything?

client: I get what you're saying about creating space to breathe, but when I'm in those overwhelming moments, it feels impossible to even notice what's happening. My thoughts are racing so fast that trying to observe them just makes me feel more out of control. It's like trying to read street signs while driving way too fast.
therapist: It sounds like those moments feel like being swept up in a whirlwind where everything moves too quickly to even catch your bearings. I wonder if, instead of trying to read every "street sign," we could start by just noticing when you're feeling that sense of speeding up—what do you think about that?
